front: Why were there serious concerns about Edward VI's age in 1547?
p1: Edward was only nine — it was feared a regent might seize power, as Richard III had done in 1483 during his nephew's minority.
p2: Edward wouldn't be able to control faction within the Council, and the image of monarchy as a strong, divine power would be challenged by the image of a child.
p3: Henry had left a divided council between reformists and conservatives — Gardiner and Norfolk's fall in 1546 already left it weighted in favour of the reformists.

front: How far did Edward's minority actually threaten stability?
p1: Not all previous minorities had ended badly — Edward was noted to be an extremely bright boy showing great promise as a ruler.
p2: Somerset quickly monopolised power using the dry stamp and the 'unfulfilled gifts' clause of Henry's will, against Henry's intention of 16 co-equal councillors.
p3: The ultimate test came in 1549 — unrest spread to over half the counties of England, the most widespread of the Tudor period, showing the minority had created a serious vacuum of authority.

front: Why was faction particularly dangerous during Edward VI's minority?
p1: In the reign of a minor there was no authority to control faction — disputes could spill over into rebellion or civil war.
p2: Somerset used his position as Lord Protector to increase his personal wealth and power, giving positions to supporters like his brother Thomas Seymour — who he later executed for treason.
p3: Other Tudor monarchs encouraged faction to ensure ministers competed for their loyalty — but managing it required a strong monarch, which a nine-year-old could not provide.

front: Why did Somerset fall from power in October 1549?
p1: Somerset's arrogant leadership created the Anti-Somerset faction — reformers and conservatives including Warwick, Wriothesley and Paget — who blamed him for encouraging the unrest of 1549.
p2: Feeling threatened, Somerset issued a general summons on 5th October for loyal subjects to defend him against the Council — seen as inciting revolt.
p3: Somerset retreated to Windsor Castle but surrendered when the King turned against him, declaring he was being kept prisoner.

front: How did Northumberland consolidate power after Somerset's fall?
p1: Facing conservative opposition, Warwick allied himself with the reformist faction and committed to further religious reform — becoming Lord President of the Council in 1550.
p2: He released Somerset and restored him to the Council, but when this proved unsuccessful had Somerset executed for treason in 1552 — the charges were likely fabricated to remove a rival.
p3: Northumberland's methods showed how dangerous minority rule was — without a strong monarch, the most ruthless faction could dominate government and eliminate opponents under cover of law.

front: Why did Northumberland and Edward attempt to alter the succession in 1553?
p1: Edward feared for the survival of his Protestant changes — Mary was a committed Catholic who had refused even his personal appeals to convert.
p2: Northumberland feared his own fall from power when Mary came to the throne, so married his son Guildford Dudley to Jane Grey to control the heir.
p3: Edward's illness progressed before Jane Grey had children, so in his own hand he crossed out 'male heirs' and named Jane Grey directly — giving the Devise a shaky legal basis.

front: Why did the Devise for the Succession fail to prevent Mary's accession?
p1: Mary had a significant power base in East Anglia — she proclaimed herself Queen on 9th July, before the Council's proclamation of Jane on the 10th.
p2: On the march north, Northumberland's army deserted him and Councillors broke ranks for Mary. He retreated to Cambridge and accepted Mary as queen on the 19th.
p3: Mary entered London to rousing popular support — popular legitimacy proved more powerful than legal manoeuvring, and Northumberland, Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were all later executed.

front: Why did Mary's gender create problems for her rule?
p1: Mary was the first Queen to rule England in her own right — many believed female rulers could not control powerful men, lead soldiers into battle or display the strength a monarch needed.
p2: John Knox wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558), comparing female rulers to 'the blind leading those who can see'.
p3: Precedent was concerning — when Matilda was named heir in the 12th century, Henry I's death led to a civil war as many nobles refused to accept female rule.

front: How far did Mary's gender actually undermine her authority as queen?
p1: Despite fears, Mary successfully managed her Council throughout her reign — faction was less serious under Mary than under Edward.
p2: During Wyatt's Rebellion Mary stayed in London against her Council's advice and delivered her Guildhall speech to rally the Londoners — proving female rulers could act with strength.
p3: The willingness of Edward and Northumberland to make Jane Grey queen shows gender was seen as less important than religion — concerns about female rule were subordinate to other political calculations.

front: Why was Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain controversial?
p1: A foreign marriage risked an unpopular influx of foreigners, England's entanglement in foreign wars, and xenophobic popular reaction — Wyatt's Rebellion broke out in January 1554 ostensibly in reaction to the marriage.
p2: Philip was Mary's personal choice — championed by Paget — bringing powerful Habsburg alliances as his father Charles V was Holy Roman Emperor. But Edward Courtenay, championed by Gardiner, was the English alternative.
p3: Ultimately the marriage ended unhappily — after Mary's phantom pregnancy, Philip rarely spent time in England. When Mary died he commented he felt 'a reasonable regret'.

front: How was the marriage to Philip managed to limit its dangers?
p1: A treaty was agreed: Philip would be named King but have no power in his own right; no Spaniards would be granted offices or lands in England.
p2: After Mary's death Philip would have no claim to the throne; England would not be entangled in Spain's wars — terms designed to reassure the English political nation.
p3: The treaty ultimately failed to prevent controversy — England was drawn into Spain's war with France, leading to the humiliating loss of Calais in 1558, the last English territory in France.

front: How effectively did Mary manage faction on her Privy Council?
p1: 'Casual councillors' were excluded from key committees in 1554; in 1555 Mary established an 'inner council' so only her most valued advisors were present.
p2: Three key figures dominated: Gardiner (cautious realist), Paget (exceptional administrator) and Cardinal Pole (zealous Catholic). Pole's return in 1554 brought dispute with Gardiner over the pace of restoration.
p3: These struggles were minor and short-lived — Gardiner's death in 1555 ensured Pole's methods won out. For the majority of Mary's reign the Council worked effectively and carried out her wishes.

front: What problems did Elizabeth inherit at the succession in 1558?
p1: Mary died having failed to produce an heir. England had lost Calais — the last English territory in France — from joining Spain's war with France. Cardinal Pole died the same day, leaving the Church without an Archbishop.
p2: Philip of Spain chose not to press his claim, preferring a Protestant England to a France-aligned Catholic one. But Henry II of France proclaimed Mary Queen of Scots as the true Queen of England.
p3: Elizabeth inherited a country divided by religion, weakened by war and debt, and faced an immediate Catholic challenge to the legitimacy of her rule.

front: What religious inheritance did Edward VI receive from Henry VIII?
p1: Henry never truly embraced Protestantism — he only embraced changes that brought him money and power, including the Dissolution of the Monasteries.
p2: The 1539 Act of Six Articles confirmed Catholic practices including Transubstantiation and clerical celibacy — England was doctrinally Catholic despite the break with Rome.
p3: The majority of the country, outside London and East Anglia, just wanted to worship as their ancestors had done for a millennium — they did not understand the differences between Catholicism and Protestantism.

front: What did the three stages of the Edwardian Reformation achieve?
p1: Stage 1 — Destruction, 1547: iconoclasm encouraged; Six Articles and Treason Act repealed; Chantries dissolved. The old had to be destroyed before the new could be installed.
p2: Stage 2 — Limbo, 1548–49: First Book of Common Prayer enforced — a vague compromise on Holy Communion that pleased nobody and prompted the Western Rebellion.
p3: Stage 3 — Formulation, 1550–53: Second Book of Common Prayer (1552) removed all Catholic practices and confirmed Communion was purely symbolic. Forty-Two Articles drawn up but never passed — Edward died in 1553.

front: How far was England Protestant by 1553 — the analytical argument?
p1: Just because de jure England was Protestant does not mean de facto this was true — six years was a small amount of time to upend 1,000 years of Catholic worship.
p2: Bishop Hooper's visitations found that of 311 Gloucester clergymen, 171 couldn't repeat the Ten Commandments and 40 couldn't find the Lord's Prayer.
p3: Evidence from wills shows little support for changes outside London and East Anglia — the rapid restoration of Catholicism under Mary suggests traditional religion still retained its popularity.

front: What were Mary's religious aims and why were they difficult to achieve?
p1: Mary aimed to undo religious changes since 1529 — restoring Papal authority, Catholic practices, Transubstantiation and dissolved monasteries — and secure Catholicism's future by marrying and having children.
p2: Advisors were concerned: Gardiner doubted restoring Papal authority; Renard warned against restoring monastic property; even Charles V and the Pope feared she would move too quickly.
p3: Parliament refused to repeal the Act of Supremacy in October 1553, and in April 1554 landowning MPs refused to reinstate the heresy laws until Mary guaranteed ex-monastic land was safe.

front: How systematic was Mary's Catholic restoration?
p1: Mary used the royal prerogative to restore the Catholic Mass. The Royal Injunctions of 1554 restored Catholic practices — Holy Days, processions and ceremonies — and deprived large numbers of married clergy.
p2: The Second Act of Repeal (November 1554) repealed all religious legislation since 1529. Over the next three years 284 Protestants were burnt — most notably Archbishop Cranmer and Bishops Hooper, Ridley and Latimer.
p3: The 12 Decrees of 1556 banned absenteeism, pluralism and simony — showing Mary was improving clerical quality, not just restoring Catholicism.

front: Why were the Marian burnings counter-productive?
p1: 284 people were burnt (51 women), mostly in the Protestant strongholds of the south-east. Large numbers attended but there is little evidence the burnings converted anyone — many viewed them as entertainment.
p2: Gardiner opposed the burnings as counter-productive — his death in 1555 meant they continued under Pole's direction. Foxe's Book of Martyrs shaped how posterity viewed the Marian regime.
p3: c.800 Protestants fled abroad, including many printers who developed an underground propaganda movement — keeping Cranmer's Prayer Book and Foxe's Book of Martyrs in circulation and radicalising the exiles with Calvinist ideas.

front: How far had England returned to Catholicism by 1558 — the analytical argument?
p1: Edward's short reign meant much of the country, especially the North, had always remained Catholic. Catholic worship returned speedily — unlike Henry and Edward, Mary faced no rebellion on the issue of religion.
p2: However five years was insufficient to enact lasting change. Over 800 clergy were deprived for failing to return to Catholic practices — though a small proportion of the total.
p3: By not producing an heir, Catholicism did not triumph. But the time it took Elizabeth to re-establish Protestantism suggests the Marian restoration had achieved significant de facto change.

front: What were the main causes of the Great Price Rise in the mid-Tudor period?
p1: Population rise — the Malthusian Crisis: from 1525–1551 the population rose from 2.3 to 3 million. Agricultural productivity could not keep pace, food prices rose, and bad harvests were worsened by the beginning of the Little Ice Age.
p2: Debasement: Henry VIII reduced the precious metal content of coinage to fund wars — prices rose to compensate. Somerset continued debasement to fund the Scottish war, worsening inflation.
p3: Enclosure transformed arable land to livestock farming for the cloth market — producing less food and increasing unemployment. Commonwealth men blamed enclosure and greedy landlords for rack renting and regrating.

front: How far did the government's response to socioeconomic problems make the situation worse?
p1: Somerset commissioned John Hales to investigate enclosures in 1548 — raising expectations he could not fulfil — while simultaneously continuing debasement to fund the Scottish war.
p2: The Vagrancy Act of 1547 condemned vagrants to two years slavery for a first offence and lifetime slavery for a second — a deeply unpopular measure showing the government's instinct was punishment rather than relief.
p3: The lack of a strong royal presence in the minority meant central government appeared weak and susceptible to rebellion — the unrest of 1549 spread to over half the counties of England.

front: How serious was the unrest of 1549?
p1: 1549 was the 'year of the many-headed monster' — unrest in over half the counties of England, the most widespread of the Tudor period. Kett's captured Norwich; the Western Rebellion besieged Exeter for a month.
p2: Thousands of soldiers were diverted from the Scottish border. The order to execute 3,000 of the Western rebels demonstrates the establishment's fear.
p3: However neither rebellion attempted to march on London — their demands were written politely to Somerset, anger directed at local gentry rather than the Crown. Ultimately both were no match for government force.

front: What were the causes of Kett's Rebellion?
p1: The unrest began when a mob attacked the enclosures of John Flowerdew, who redirected the protest to Robert Kett — another gentleman who had also enclosed land. Rebels' demands centred on enclosure and high rents, and absent or uneducated clergy.
p2: 16,000 rebels met in July 1549, marched on Norwich, camped at Mousehold Heath and stormed the city. Somerset's commissions on enclosure had raised hopes he was the champion of the poor.
p3: In Norfolk 6% owned 60% of the land — the rebellion reflected genuine and extreme economic inequality, not just political opportunism.

front: Why did Kett's Rebellion fail and what does this reveal about mid-Tudor unrest?
p1: Warwick arrived with 12,000 well-trained troops from the Scottish war and massacred the rebels at Dussindale — 3,000 killed, 49 leaders executed for treason.
p2: Kett made the fatal error of abandoning his well-defended camp at Mousehold Heath to meet Warwick at Dussindale on open ground.
p3: The rebellion reveals the limits of mid-Tudor unrest — rebels were well-organised with legitimate grievances but lacked military experience, national coordination, and any intention of overthrowing the Crown.

front: What were the causes of the Western Rebellion of 1549?
p1: The murder of William Body in 1548 — tasked with supervising iconoclasm in Cornwall — and opposition to the First Book of Common Prayer triggered the rebellion. Many Cornishmen were more familiar with Latin than English.
p2: The demands were almost entirely religious — drawn up by literate local clergy. But evidence of excluded demands about high taxes and rents, and the chant 'Kill all the gentlemen!' at Bodmin, shows economic grievances also existed.
p3: The rebellion was primarily religious unlike Kett's which was primarily economic — but both shared a backdrop of socioeconomic grievance and were products of Somerset's failure to manage the Reformation or the economic crisis effectively.

front: How threatening was the Western Rebellion and why did it fail?
p1: The rebels besieged Exeter for a month and attacked gentry at St Michael's Mount, Bodmin and Trematon Castle. Government forces of 8,000 led by Lord John Russell defeated the rebels at Sampford Courtenay — over 3,000 executed.
p2: The rebellion failed due to no clear leadership — different sections attacked different targets, unlike the more organised Kett's Rebellion.
p3: Though serious enough to require royal suppression, the rebels never attempted to march on London. The 'many-headed monster' of 1549 showed that the combination of minority, economic crisis and religious change had made England difficult to govern without decisive royal authority.

front: What were the causes of Wyatt's Rebellion in 1554?
p1: The ostensible cause was Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain — concerns over a foreign marriage, patronage going to the Spanish, and England being dragged into Habsburg wars. The timing, immediately after the marriage was proposed in parliament, supports this.
p2: However xenophobia may have masked other causes. The rebellion began in Protestant Kent — part of the plot was to replace Mary with Elizabeth. Many leaders had lost positions at court due to their faith.
p3: The collapse of the cloth trade created unemployment in Kent. Government chronicler John Proctor blamed religion — but he was unlikely to accept popular opposition to Philip.

front: How serious a threat was Wyatt's Rebellion to Mary's reign?
p1: Government soldiers deserted Norfolk and joined Wyatt's forces declaring 'We are all Englishmen!', and Wyatt reached the gates of London — if the Londoners had opened the city gates the rebellion could have succeeded.
p2: Only one of the planned four forces actually rose — the other leaders got cold feet. The rebellion was poorly coordinated and lacked popular support outside Kent.
p3: Mary's decisive Guildhall speech secured the Londoners' loyalty. Wyatt and leaders were executed; Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower but released after Wyatt refused to implicate her under torture.

front: What were the main religious pressures Elizabeth faced in 1558?
p1: Returning Marian exiles had been radicalised by Calvinist and Zwinglian ideas — denying any role for the monarch in the Church. The powerful bishops Elizabeth inherited from Mary were all Catholics. Much of the population, especially in the North, had never truly left Catholicism.
p2: Spain and France were the two richest Catholic powers — fortunately the Habsburg-Valois rivalry meant they despised each other. Elizabeth's political future depended on this rivalry continuing.
p3: Mary Queen of Scots was married to the French Dauphin and Henry II presented her as the true Queen of England. Many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce.

front: What did the Elizabethan Religious Settlement establish and why was it a via media?
p1: The Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth Supreme Governor of the Church and repealed Mary's heresy laws. The Act of Uniformity enforced Cranmer's 1552 Book of Common Prayer — but omitted the 'Black Rubric' denying Transubstantiation, leaving communion deliberately ambiguous.
p2: Holy Communion wording drew from both 1552 and 1548 Prayer Books, allowing open interpretation. Everyone must attend Church of England services on a Sunday — recusancy fine of 1 shilling.
p3: Elizabeth called it Via Media — 'the middle way'. She promised she 'would not open windows unto men's souls' — demanding only outward conformity, not inner belief.

front: How serious was the challenge of getting the Religious Settlement through Parliament?
p1: Catholic bishops and lay nobles in the House of Lords threatened to oppose and alter the settlement — particularly objecting to making Elizabeth 'Head of the Church'.
p2: Elizabeth prorogued parliament over Easter 1559, arrested two vocal critics — the Bishops of Lincoln and Winchester — and compromised by adopting the title 'Supreme Governor' instead.
p3: The Settlement passed the House of Lords by just three votes. Elizabeth then removed the Marian bishops when they refused to swear the Oath of Loyalty.

front: How did Puritans attempt to change the Religious Settlement through Parliament?
p1: In 1571 Walter Strickland attempted to alter the Book of Common Prayer to remove vestments and kneeling at communion. Summoned before the Privy Council for infringing the Royal Prerogative, he was barred from parliament.
p2: In 1586 Anthony Cope MP made a radical 'bill and book' proposal — replacing the Book of Common Prayer with the Genevan Prayer Book and removing the episcopacy. Cope and four supporters were sent to the Tower. The bill was defeated.
p3: Elizabeth consistently framed religious matters as part of the Royal Prerogative — beyond parliamentary competence. Puritan MPs never forced lasting change through Parliament.

front: How did Puritans challenge the settlement from within the Church and through popular appeals?
p1: The Vestiarian Controversy: Puritans despised vestments. Parker compromised in his 1566 Advertisements — but 37 clergymen who refused lost their jobs. Cartwright gave Presbyterian lectures at Cambridge in 1570 denouncing Church hierarchy — he lost his professorship.
p2: Field and Wilcox published the 'Admonition to Parliament' (1572) calling for the end of episcopacy. The Marprelate Tracts (1588–89) made vicious attacks on bishops — but alienated moderates.
p3: Separatist movements were suppressed — Robert Browne's 1581 Brownist Church in Norwich, and Henry Barrow and John Greenwood's 1590s movement — the leaders were arrested and executed in 1593.

front: How successfully did Elizabeth's three archbishops defend the Religious Settlement?
p1: Matthew Parker (1559–75): a moderate not radicalised by Marian exile. Oversaw the 39 Articles at the 1563 Convocation — defeating Puritan attempts by a single vote — and reached compromise during the Vestiarian Controversy.
p2: Edmund Grindal (1575–83): a former Marian exile sympathetic to Puritans. Refused to suppress prophesyings in 1576, was suspended by Elizabeth in 1577 and confined to house arrest until his death — the only archbishop to openly defy her.
p3: John Whitgift (1583–1604): used the Court of High Commission and Three Articles to remove around 300 Puritan clergy. Showed determined repression could contain but not eliminate the Puritan challenge.

front: Why was the Catholic threat limited in the first decade of Elizabeth's reign?
p1: Elizabeth's relative tolerance limited overt challenge. The heresy laws were repealed — the sole recusancy punishment was a 1 shilling fine. Many Church Papists simply attended Church of England services before attending secret Catholic services. Elizabeth 'would not open windows unto men's souls'.
p2: Philip of Spain persuaded Pope Pius IV not to excommunicate Elizabeth in 1563 — Philip feared France gaining control of England if Mary Queen of Scots came to the throne.
p3: The Habsburg-Valois rivalry prevented coordinated Catholic action — England was not a high enough priority to overcome their mutual hostility.

front: How did the arrival of Mary Queen of Scots in 1568 transform the Catholic threat?
p1: Mary was Elizabeth's cousin and next in line — if she succeeded she would likely restore Catholicism. Many English Catholics already viewed her as the true Queen. Her arrival in the Catholic North provided a figurehead around which plots would ferment.
p2: A plot to marry Mary to the Duke of Norfolk triggered the Rising of the North — the northern earls captured Durham and held Catholic mass in the Cathedral. But no other Catholic nobility answered the summons; a royal army marched north and Elizabeth executed 450 rebels.
p3: In 1570 Pope Pius V issued his Papal bull Regnans in Excelsis excommunicating Elizabeth — Catholics were now absolved of any loyalty to her. This transformed passive non-conformity into active potential treachery.

front: What were the main Catholic plots and how were they managed?
p1: 1571 Ridolfi Plot: Norfolk, Pope and Philip II to marry Mary to Norfolk and provoke a Catholic uprising — discovered by Cecil. Norfolk executed 1572, but Elizabeth resisted calls to execute Mary. 1583 Throckmorton Plot: to liberate Mary, involving the Duke of Guise, Philip II and seminary priests — uncovered by Walsingham.
p2: 1584 Bond of Association: the Privy Council pledged to kill anyone linked to future plots — showing the government taking the initiative. 1586 Babington Plot: Walsingham discovered evidence directly implicating Mary herself.
p3: The combined pressure of the Lords, Commons and Privy Council following Babington forced Elizabeth's hand — Mary was executed in February 1587. After Mary's execution Catholic plots became far less dangerous, having lost their potential monarch.

front: How did seminary priests and Jesuits transform the Catholic threat from the 1570s?
p1: William Allen's 'English College' at Douai produced the first seminary priests, who arrived in England from 1574. By 1585, 279 had travelled to England. From the 1580s Jesuits also arrived — around 650 in total, sheltered by Catholic gentry in priest holes.
p2: The priests revitalised English Catholicism but gave the government justification for treating all Catholics as potential traitors — making it increasingly difficult for moderate 'Church Papists' to maintain their ambiguous position.
p3: Government response escalated: 1581 — recusancy fines raised to £20 a month; 1585 — all Catholic priests expelled, harbouring a priest punishable by death. 133 seminary priests and Jesuits were executed.

front: Why did the Catholic challenge ultimately fail?
p1: Elizabeth's tolerance meant most Catholics had little reason to actively oppose the settlement — the 1 shilling recusancy fine was manageable. Her refusal to create martyrs meant the majority had no need to overtly oppose the settlement.
p2: The Pope's 1570 excommunication was too little, too late — after 11 years of the settlement and after the Northern Rising had been crushed. The Habsburg-Valois rivalry prevented coordinated Catholic action.
p3: Elizabeth's 45-year reign was decisive — the Catholic establishment from Mary's reign died out and the new generation of gentry, nobility and clergy all grew up under Elizabeth's settlement. The failure of the Spanish Armada in 1588 was a major propaganda boost for Protestantism.

front: How did the Elizabethan system of government operate?
p1: The monarch derived power from God — all legislation required Royal Assent and the Royal Prerogative covered religion, succession and foreign policy. The Privy Council — maximum 20 members — met several times a week and was dominated for most of the reign by William Cecil.
p2: Parliament was called ten times during Elizabeth's reign — passing permanent legislation and crucially approving taxation. MPs in the Commons tended to be gentry; the Lords included Lords Temporal and Lords Spiritual.
p3: The Privy Council managed parliament by setting the parliamentary agenda, influencing the election of the Speaker and promoting its supporters as MPs.

front: Who were the key figures on Elizabeth's Privy Council?
p1: William Cecil (Lord Burghley from 1571): principal advisor until 1598. Secretary of State until 1572, then Lord Treasurer. Drafted the Religious Settlement, created an intelligence service, ran the Privy Council. Cautious and pragmatic.
p2: Robert Dudley (Earl of Leicester from 1564): Elizabeth's favourite — charming, charismatic, promoted more for personality than skill. A devout Puritan who championed military intervention abroad. His wife Amy Robsart died in mysterious circumstances in 1560.
p3: Sir Francis Walsingham: took over the intelligence service and Secretary of State in 1573. A devout Puritan who hated Mary Queen of Scots. Thomas Howard, Duke of Norfolk: the only Duke — executed in 1572 for the Ridolfi Plot.

front: How effectively did Elizabeth manage faction on her Privy Council?
p1: Elizabeth stayed aloof of faction and encouraged disputes to get wider debate. By delaying decisions she showed favour to no particular faction. She used her gender to manage loyalty — councillors competed for her affection.
p2: 1565–66: Leicester came into dispute with Norfolk's faction. Elizabeth ended it by making clear she would not marry Leicester. 1578–85: the Dutch Revolt divided the Council between Leicester and Walsingham (intervention) and Burghley (caution).
p3: Mary Queen of Scots united the Council against Elizabeth — they repeatedly petitioned for her execution and agreed the Bond of Association in 1584, pledging to kill anyone linked to future plots.

front: What tools did Elizabeth use to manage Parliament?
p1: Elizabeth could dissolve a parliament she disapproved of and call a new one with newly elected MPs, or prorogue parliament — suspending it while the Privy Council put pressure on MPs to change position.
p2: Elizabeth and the Privy Council influenced the choice of Speaker who controlled debates. If a disapproved bill passed both Houses, Elizabeth could use her Royal Veto. As a last resort, she could arrest MPs challenging her prerogative as traitors.
p3: However aggressive use of royal power could increase parliamentary opposition — Elizabeth preferred management through influence rather than outright confrontation.

front: What were the main areas of conflict between Elizabeth and Parliament?
p1: Religion: Strickland's Bill (1571) and Cope's 'bill and book' (1586) both attempted to alter the Religious Settlement and were blocked as infringements of the Royal Prerogative. Peter Wentworth MP repeatedly argued Parliament should freely discuss religion and succession — in 1576 the House of Commons itself sent him to the Tower.
p2: Marriage: Parliament presented petitions in 1559 and 1563. In 1566 Cecil organised a parliamentary delegation following Elizabeth's near-fatal Smallpox. Elizabeth reduced her subsidy by 1/3 but reaffirmed succession was part of her Royal Prerogative.
p3: Neale argued the relationship was one of conflict; revisionist Elton argued it was mainly co-operation — both Crown and Parliament shared aims for stability and the Protestant settlement.

front: Why did Elizabeth refuse to marry or name a successor?
p1: Elizabeth resented sharing power with a man and described naming a successor as 'buried alive' — it would mean enemies developing plots around that successor. As she grew older, key ministers would abandon her for a named successor.
p2: The choice was almost impossible: a fellow monarch risked foreign entanglement as Mary I's marriage to Philip had proved; foreigners were unpopular; an English noble could create resentment and faction; almost all candidates were Catholic. A male monarch could have used marriage to forge alliances — e.g. Archduke Charles of Austria as a Habsburg ally — without surrendering sovereignty. Elizabeth could not.
p3: Despite never naming a successor, her tacit acknowledgement that James VI of Scotland would succeed meant the issue was manageable. Her letters to James indicated he would be King — he did not oppose his mother's execution in 1587.

front: What was the impact of Elizabeth's refusal to resolve the succession question?
p1: In 1579 John Stubbs wrote a pamphlet criticising the Alençon match — Elizabeth had all copies burned and his right hand removed. The crowd described Stubbs as 'a true Englishman', showing public support for his position.
p2: The Bond of Association (1584) pledged to kill anyone linked to future plots against Elizabeth. Combined pressure of Lords, Commons and Privy Council following the Babington Plot forced Elizabeth's hand — Mary was executed in 1587.
p3: Despite never naming a successor, Elizabeth's tacit acknowledgement that James VI would succeed meant the issue was ultimately manageable. The peaceful succession of James I in 1603 vindicated Elizabeth's long-term strategy.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What was the financial situation Elizabeth inherited in 1558?
p1: Elizabeth inherited a debt of £227,000 from Mary's involvement in the war with France, largely owed to the Antwerp Exchange at 14% interest. Gresham identified three problems: debasement of coinage; cost of war; and the Hanseatic League's control over wool exports.
p2: Mary had introduced the revised Book of Rates which boosted customs revenue, and the Exchequer now collected three-quarters of Crown revenue. Elizabeth inherited able administrators in Gresham and Lord Treasurer William Paulet.
p3: Gresham's advice was to maintain an excellent credit rating by swiftly repaying debt and avoiding loans in peacetime — allowing Elizabeth to raise loans quickly at favourable rates when war made it necessary.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How successfully did Elizabeth manage Crown finances before the war with Spain?
p1: By 1576 the Marian debt had been cleared; by 1584 Elizabeth had accrued a surplus of £300,000. Achieved by avoiding her father's excessive lifestyle, not spending on building projects, going on 'progress' at courtiers' expense, and avoiding war.
p2: However her management of ordinary revenue was less impressive — she sold significant Crown lands (bringing in £600,000 but depleting long-term income), the Book of Rates was not regularly revised, and Custom Farmers led to widespread corruption.
p3: Taxes in England were amongst the lowest in Europe. The financial success before 1585 was real but fragile — dependent on continued peace and prudent spending, not structural reform of revenue collection.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What caused inflation during Elizabeth's reign?
p1: Population rise from c.2.7 to c.4 million between 1547 and 1603 meant demand outstripped supply. Poor harvests — made common by the Little Ice Age — reduced supply further. By the 1560s, average food prices were triple those of Henry VII's reign.
p2: Bullion: gold and silver from the New World reduced the value of precious metals across Europe — making coinage less valuable and pushing up prices.
p3: Contemporaries blamed enclosure and greedy landlords — they did not understand how rising population affected supply and demand. This misdiagnosis meant the government could not tackle the underlying cause.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How effectively did the government respond to inflation?
p1: Gresham's recoinage of 1560 called in debased coins and removed base alloys — but prices did not go down: merchants simply set the same prices, or higher.
p2: Elizabeth encouraged fasting during Lent and 'fish days' on Wednesdays and Fridays to limit demand. The 1586 Book of Orders prohibited hoarding of grain — demand management rather than structural solutions.
p3: Ultimately the government could not tackle inflation — they lacked understanding of how rising population affected supply and demand. Inflation was a structural problem no Tudor government had the economic tools to solve.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What was the financial impact of the war with Spain from 1585?
p1: Elizabeth's surplus of £300,000 was used almost entirely in the first year of war. The Treaty of Nonsuch committed £126,000 per year to support the Dutch rebels. Total war cost: £4.5 million — £2m in the Netherlands, £2m in Ireland, £500,000 for Henry of Navarre, £160,000 against the Armada.
p2: Elizabeth was forced to sell more Crown lands in the 1590s and resort to monopolies as patronage — contributing to price rises and creating dissatisfaction in Parliament.
p3: Some benefits: Drake's 1587 Cadiz raid brought £140,000; Flemings and Huguenots brought improved manufacturing skills. But these could not compensate for the enormous drain on the Exchequer.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How successfully did Elizabeth expand overseas trade?
p1: The Dutch Revolt and war with Spain collapsed the Antwerp cloth market — new markets were needed. New companies were established: Muscovy Company (1555); Eastland Company (1579); Levant Company (1580); East India Company (1600).
p2: In the New World, Hawkins created the Triangular Slave Trade in 1562 — Elizabeth herself invested. Raleigh's attempts to create colonies at Roanoke Island failed. Spain and Portugal dominated the New World — English activity was largely limited to piracy.
p3: Success was limited — the Hanseatic League resisted English advances in the Baltic; the East India Company had little value in Elizabeth's lifetime; no colonies were established. England remained dependent on the European markets the war had disrupted.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: What caused poverty and vagrancy to grow during Elizabeth's reign?
p1: The growing population created a labour surplus — employers could lower wages while landlords raised rents. Combined with inflation this created large amounts of poverty. Contemporaries blamed enclosure and greedy landlords, though the real cause was population growth.
p2: The wars with Spain and Ireland compounded the problem — soldiers and sailors were discharged far from home, often with no pay and serious injuries, adding to the pool of destitute vagrants.
p3: Elizabethans feared vagrants intensely — viewed as disease-spreaders and criminals. The government feared they encouraged social unrest. By 1600, in some areas over 70% of available arable land was enclosed.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
front: How did government attitudes to poverty change during Elizabeth's reign?
p1: Early legislation was punitive: the 1563 Alms Act created a voluntary Poor Rate; the 1572 Vagabonds Act made contributions compulsory but enacted severe penalties including whipping, mutilation and execution.
p2: A gradual shift occurred: the 1576 Act for the Relief of the Poor provided 'able-bodied' poor with work in a House of Correction — the first recognition that the 'undeserving poor' required help, not just punishment.
p3: The 1601 Poor Law made the state permanently responsible for providing poor relief and codified the distinction between 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor — provisions lasting until the mid-19th century.

front: What were the main theatres of the war with Spain and what did the Spanish Armada achieve?
p1: War was fought in the Netherlands (supporting Dutch rebels), at sea (Sea Dogs raiding the Spanish Main), in France (supporting Protestant Henry of Navarre) and in Ireland (Spain supported Tyrone's Rebellion).
p2: The Spanish Armada of 1588 — 130 ships and 57,000 men — was defeated: English fireships at Calais scattered the fleet; the Battle of Gravelines inflicted losses; storms destroyed much of the remainder. Elizabeth's Tilbury speech was a major propaganda triumph.
p3: Victory came at huge cost — forced loans of £75,000 from the nobility and £56,000 from the City of London. After the Armada, failure at sea was common — Drake's 'English Armada' of 1589 was an unmitigated disaster.

front: What was the domestic impact of the war with Spain?
p1: The £4.5 million cost destroyed Elizabeth's surplus almost immediately. She was forced to sell more Crown lands and resort to monopolies as patronage — contributing to price rises and creating dissatisfaction in Parliament.
p2: The war forced Elizabeth to call Parliament more frequently — five of her ten Parliaments were called after 1585, giving MPs leverage to raise grievances over monopolies, purveyance and the succession.
p3: The war exacerbated faction between the conservative Cecils and the more hawkish Essex — creating a lack of coherent policy. Elizabeth used her Golden Speech to appease MPs' anger over monopolies in the 1601 Parliament.

front: Why was Ireland such a serious problem during Elizabeth's later years?
p1: English power was only felt in the Pale around Dublin. Elizabeth's unwillingness to commit funds to a long-term strategy led to poorly implemented policies under ever-changing Lord Deputies. Ireland remained Catholic as English power was too weak to enforce Protestantism.
p2: Tyrone's Rebellion (1594–1603) was the most dangerous — coming during the war with Spain when resources were stretched. Tyrone gained national support and won at Yellow Ford in 1598. Essex led 16,000 men but never fought a battle and returned to London without permission.
p3: Lord Mountjoy forced Tyrone's surrender days after Elizabeth's death in 1603 — Tyrone fled, allowing Ulster to be colonised by Protestants. Total cost: £2 million — a devastating drain on already strained finances.

front: How did Essex rise to prominence at Elizabeth's court?
p1: Essex rose to court as Leicester's godson — his wit, eloquence and dashing personality made him a favourite of the ageing Elizabeth. Raised to the Privy Council in 1593 due to personality more than political skill.
p2: Essex frequently acted unilaterally — joining Drake's 1589 Armada against Elizabeth's orders; capturing Cadiz in 1596 which made him enormously popular. But in 1596 Robert Cecil became Secretary of State while Essex was at Cadiz, securing control over government.
p3: Essex's flamboyant arrogance clashed with the more pragmatic Robert Cecil. The war exacerbated faction between the conservative Cecils and the hawkish Essex, creating a lack of coherent policy.

front: Why did Essex's Rebellion of 1601 fail and what were its consequences?
p1: Whilst in house arrest Essex lost his monopoly over sweet wines. He controversially commissioned a performance of Shakespeare's Richard II — depicting the deposition of a childless monarch. Elizabeth had banned this play.
p2: Essex gathered supporters in the City of London but most got cold feet — the rebellion was poorly planned and almost immediately defeated. Essex and just 5 supporters were executed in 1601.
p3: The rebellion revealed that personal popularity was no substitute for control of government machinery. Cecil's careful accumulation of institutional power proved decisive — from 1601 his faction controlled government unopposed, managing the smooth transition to James I in 1603.

front: What caused the socioeconomic crisis of the 1590s?
p1: A series of bad harvests from 1594–98 doubled the average price of wheat. The Malthusian Crisis continued — population continued to outstrip food production. The death rate increased by 50% at the peak of the crisis in 1595–7.
p2: The wars with Spain and Ireland compounded the problem: unprecedented taxation in 1589 and 1593; monopolies raising prices; discharged soldiers adding to the numbers of destitute vagrants.
p3: Between 1595–98 food riots erupted in Kent, Sussex, Somerset and Norfolk. Elizabeth's granting of monopolies to favourites increased prices on staple goods — combining with harvest failure to create the most serious socioeconomic crisis of her reign.

front: How effectively did the government respond to the socioeconomic crisis of the 1590s?
p1: The Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 — a protest against enclosure at the peak of the food crisis — was quickly suppressed. The five ringleaders were executed. In the end only four people actually turned up — the threat of unrest was greater than actual unrest.
p2: The 1597 Tillage Act reversed enclosure carried out since 1588. The 1601 Poor Law codified the distinction between 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor and made the state permanently responsible for poor relief — lasting until the mid-19th century.
p3: The crisis revealed the structural limits of Elizabethan government — it could respond to disorder but not prevent its underlying causes. Norwich's community fund, inspired by Kett's rebellion, was a model for what a determined local authority could achieve.

front: How did Elizabeth manage her reputation in her later years?
p1: As Elizabeth entered her 60s her looks diminished — blackened teeth, grey hair hidden by a red wig, a pockmarked face from smallpox. In 1596 the Privy Council ordered the destruction of any 'unseemly' portraits — all had to be based on Nicholas Hilliard's agreed flattering version.
p2: Portraits like the Rainbow Portrait used heavy symbolism — she holds a rainbow (peace and divine favour); on her dress are eyes and ears (she sees and hears all). Every year on November 17, Accession Day Tilts were lavishly celebrated. Spenser's The Faerie Queene glorified Elizabeth as 'Gloriana'.
p3: However scandals undermined her image at court, the nobility were sometimes reluctant to accompany her on progress, and the 1590s unrest led some to comment 'We shall never have a merry world while the queen liveth'. Yet her 1601 Golden Speech was seen as a glorious end to an era.

front: What did Henry VIII's Third Act of Succession (1543) establish?
p1: If Edward died without heirs the throne would pass to Mary then Elizabeth — though the illegitimacy of both was never reversed.
p2: Henry instructed a Regency Council of 16 members, balanced between reformists (Seymour) and conservatives (Gardiner and Norfolk).
p3: Gardiner and Norfolk's fall from grace in 1546 meant the Council was already weighted in favour of the reformists before Edward came to the throne.

front: What fears existed about Edward VI's minority?
p1: Edward was only nine — it was feared a regent might seize power, as Richard III had done in 1483 during his nephew's minority.
p2: Edward wouldn't be able to control faction within the Council and the image of monarchy as a strong, divine power would be challenged by a child.
p3: However not all previous minorities had ended badly — Edward was noted to be an extremely bright boy showing great promise as a ruler.

front: Who were the key factions on Edward VI's Regency Council?
p1: Reformists: Somerset and John Dudley, Earl of Warwick. Conservatives: Thomas Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton.
p2: The reformist faction, led by Somerset, dominated the Regency Council by 1547 — he gave positions to supporters like his brother Thomas Seymour, whom he later executed for treason.
p3: As Lord Protector Somerset used his position to increase his personal wealth and power, resulting in criticism from opponents and even former supporters.

front: How did Somerset seize power after Henry VIII's death?
p1: Seymour and Paget conspired using the dry stamp and the 'unfulfilled gifts' clause of Henry's will to increase their power.
p2: Seymour was made Duke of Somerset, Lord Protector and predominant figure on the new Regency Council.
p3: Somerset's rise was unopposed — some suggested a leading figure would be more effective than 16 co-equal councillors.

front: What created the Anti-Somerset faction?
p1: Somerset's arrogant and dominating leadership united reformers and conservatives including Warwick, Wriothesley and Paget against him.
p2: They feared his apparent sympathy for the commoners and enclosure had encouraged the unrest of 1549.
p3: Edward himself disliked Somerset's control — he was allowed no influence at all over his own government.

front: What were the key events of Somerset's fall in October 1549?
p1: Feeling threatened, Somerset issued a general summons on 5th October for loyal subjects to defend him against the Council — seen as inciting revolt.
p2: Somerset retreated to Windsor Castle with the King but was forced to surrender when Edward turned against him, declaring he was being kept prisoner.
p3: Somerset was arrested, then executed for treason in 1552 — the evidence suggests the charges were fabricated by Northumberland to remove a rival.

front: How did Northumberland secure power after Somerset's fall?
p1: Facing conservative opposition from the Earls of Arundel and Southampton, Warwick allied with the reformist faction — becoming Lord President of the Council in 1550.
p2: He released Somerset and restored him to the Council hoping to use his influence, but when this failed had him executed for treason in 1552.
p3: The accusations of treason against Somerset were likely fabricated — removing him as a potential rival for Northumberland.

front: Why did Edward and Northumberland devise the Devise for the Succession?
p1: Edward feared for his Protestant changes — Mary was a committed Catholic who had refused even his personal appeals to convert.
p2: Northumberland feared his own fall from power when Mary came to the throne.
p3: There is debate over who was more responsible — Edward was 15 and taking an active role in government by 1553.

front: What were the key terms of the Devise for the Succession?
p1: The Devise originally named the future male children of Jane Grey as heir — Northumberland married his son Guildford Dudley to Jane Grey to control the heir.
p2: Edward's illness progressed before Jane Grey had children — in his own hand he crossed out 'male heirs' and named Jane Grey directly.
p3: To preserve his power Northumberland married his son Guildford Dudley to Jane Grey, hoping to control the future king.

front: Why did the Devise for the Succession fail?
p1: Mary had a significant power base in East Anglia — she proclaimed herself Queen on 9th July, before the Council's proclamation of Jane on the 10th.
p2: On the march north, Northumberland's army deserted him and Councillors broke ranks for Mary — he retreated to Cambridge and accepted Mary as queen on the 19th.
p3: Mary entered London to rousing popular support — Northumberland, Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were all later executed.

front: Why was female rule considered a problem in 1553?
p1: Mary was the first Queen to rule England in her own right — many believed female rulers could not control powerful men, lead soldiers into battle or display the strength a monarch needed.
p2: In the 12th century, Matilda, daughter of Henry I, was named heir — Henry's death led to a civil war as nobles refused to accept female rule.
p3: John Knox wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558), comparing female rulers to 'the blind leading those who can see'.

front: What evidence shows Mary's gender did not prevent effective rule?
p1: Despite fears, Mary successfully managed her Council throughout her reign — faction was less serious under Mary than under Edward.
p2: During Wyatt's Rebellion Mary stayed in London against her Council's advice — her Guildhall speech secured the Londoners' loyalty and crushed the rebellion.
p3: The willingness of Edward and Northumberland to make Jane Grey queen shows gender was less important than religion in political calculations.

front: Who were the two candidates for Mary's hand in marriage and why was the choice controversial?
p1: Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon — championed by Gardiner as a powerful English noble with royal blood who would secure Mary's reign.
p2: Philip of Spain — championed by Paget and Mary's personal choice; his father Charles V was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain, but it risked a xenophobic popular reaction.
p3: If Mary married an English noble this would lead to division and faction; a foreign prince risked England's entanglement in foreign wars.

front: What were the key terms of the marriage treaty between Mary and Philip?
p1: Philip would be named King but have no power in his own right; no Spaniards would be granted offices or lands in England.
p2: After Mary's death Philip would have no claim to the throne; England would not be entangled in Spain's wars.
p3: Despite these terms, Wyatt's rebellion broke out in January 1554 ostensibly in reaction to the marriage — and England was eventually drawn into Spain's war with France, leading to the loss of Calais in 1558.

front: Who were the three key figures on Mary's Privy Council?
p1: Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester — a long-standing committed Catholic and cautious realist. Had been imprisoned by Edward in 1551.
p2: William Paget — an eminent political survivor and exceptional administrator who had served Henry, Edward and Mary. Not committed to religious change.
p3: Cardinal Reginald Pole — a fiercely zealous Catholic returned from exile. His return in 1554 brought dispute with Gardiner over the pace of restoration — Gardiner stressed caution; Pole favoured persecution.

front: How effectively did Mary manage her Privy Council?
p1: 'Casual councillors' were excluded from key committees in 1554; in 1555 Mary established an 'inner council' of only her most valued advisors.
p2: The dispute between Gardiner and Pole over the pace of Catholic restoration was minor and short-lived — Gardiner's death in 1555 ensured Pole's methods won out.
p3: For the majority of Mary's reign the Council worked effectively and carried out her wishes — faction was far less serious than under Edward.

front: What problems did Elizabeth inherit at the succession in November 1558?
p1: Mary died on 17th November 1558 — Cardinal Pole died the same day, leaving the Church without an Archbishop of Canterbury. Mary had failed to produce an heir.
p2: England had lost Calais — the last English territory in France — from joining Spain's war with France. Philip of Spain chose not to press his claim, preferring a Protestant England to a France-aligned Catholic one.
p3: Henry II of France proclaimed Mary Queen of Scots the true Queen of England — many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce.

front: What religious situation did Edward VI inherit from Henry VIII?
p1: Despite Henry's Break from Rome, he never truly embraced Protestantism — he only embraced changes that brought him money and power, including the Dissolution of the Monasteries.
p2: The 1539 Act of Six Articles confirmed Catholic practices including Transubstantiation and clerical celibacy — England was doctrinally Catholic despite the break with Rome.
p3: The majority of the country, outside London and East Anglia, just wanted to worship as their ancestors had done for a millennium.

front: What happened in Stage 1 — Destruction (1547) of the Edwardian Reformation?
p1: Royal injunctions were issued encouraging iconoclasm in churches across England.
p2: The Six Articles were repealed — removing the Catholic doctrine set out by Henry. The Treason Act was repealed — it was no longer treason to preach dissenting religious views.
p3: The Chantries were dissolved — seen as superstitious forms of Catholic worship, and also bringing in revenue and land for the Crown.

front: What happened in Stage 2 — Limbo (1548–49) of the Edwardian Reformation?
p1: The repeal of the Treason Laws opened a Pandora's Box of radical ideas — Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism were all being preached, creating confusion.
p2: Cranmer published the First Book of Common Prayer in December 1548 — enforced nationwide by the First Act of Uniformity. It was deliberately vague on Holy Communion and did not please anyone.
p3: This Prayer Book prompted the Western Rebellion in the West Country. The Act of Uniformity encouraged some Protestant practices but many old Catholic practices like belief in Purgatory remained.

front: What happened in Stage 3 — Formulation (1550–53) of the Edwardian Reformation?
p1: A new ordinal (1550) allowed leading Catholic clergy to be replaced with Protestants. A new Treason Act made it an offence to question the Royal Supremacy.
p2: In 1552, Cranmer published the Second Book of Common Prayer — much more radical than the first, removing all Catholic practices and confirming Communion was purely symbolic.
p3: The Forty-Two Articles (1552) outlining the key doctrines of Edward's Church were drawn up but never passed by Parliament — Edward died in 1553. Nevertheless by 1553, de jure England was a Protestant country.

front: What evidence shows the Edwardian Reformation had limited de facto impact?
p1: Bishop Hooper's visitations in Gloucester found that of 311 clergymen, 171 couldn't repeat the Ten Commandments and 40 couldn't find the Lord's Prayer.
p2: There was opposition at grass roots — unrest in Devon, Cornwall, Yorkshire, Hampshire and Oxfordshire. Repeated efforts to campaign against images in churches (1547, 1548, 1549) demonstrated the difficulties of imposing change.
p3: Evidence from people's wills shows little support for the changes outside London and East Anglia. Many people simply conformed because they were told to.

front: What specific evidence shows England was not truly Protestant by 1553?
p1: Just because de jure England was Protestant does not mean de facto this was true — six years was a small amount of time to upend 1,000 years of Catholic worship.
p2: The repeal of the Treason Act allowed multiple forms of radical Protestantism as well as old Catholic practices to be practiced. The lack of punishment for non-attendance encouraged non-conformity.
p3: The rapid restoration of Catholicism under Mary suggests traditional religion still retained its popularity — making Mary's task much easier.

front: What were Mary's religious aims?
p1: Undo religious changes since 1529 — restore Papal authority, Catholic practices, Transubstantiation and dissolved monasteries.
p2: Secure a long-term future for Catholicism by marrying and having children. Ensure the Catholic religion was abided by across the country.
p3: Her advisors were concerned about feasibility — Gardiner doubted restoring Papal authority; Renard warned against restoring monastic property; even Charles V and the Pope feared she would move too quickly.

front: What obstacles did Mary face in Parliament over religious restoration?
p1: Parliament met in October 1553 but refused to repeal the Act of Supremacy — suggesting anti-Papal feeling. It did pass the 1st Act of Repeal restoring the religious situation of 1547.
p2: Mary used the royal prerogative to get rid of the Second Act of Uniformity and restore the Catholic Mass.
p3: In April 1554 landowning MPs refused to reinstate the heresy laws until Mary guaranteed ex-monastic land was safe. In November Mary accepted — the heresy laws were then revived.

front: What specific measures did Mary take to restore Catholicism?
p1: The Royal Injunctions of 1554 restored Catholic practices — Holy Days, processions and ceremonies — and led to the deprivation of large numbers of married clergy.
p2: The Second Act of Repeal (November 1554) repealed all religious legislation since 1529 — protecting property rights of those who had bought church land since 1536.
p3: The 12 Decrees of 1556 banned absenteeism, pluralism and simony — improving clerical quality, not just restoring Catholicism.

front: What were the key facts about the Marian burnings?
p1: 284 people were burnt at the stake (51 women) from February 1555 until Mary's death in 1558 — the first was biblical translator John Rogers. Most took place in the Protestant strongholds of the south-east.
p2: In October 1555, Bishops Ridley and Latimer were burned at Oxford. In March 1556 Cranmer was burned — he had recanted Protestantism but at the stake reversed his recantation and denounced the Pope.
p3: Gardiner opposed the burnings as counter-productive — his death in 1555 meant they continued under Pole. Large numbers attended the burnings but there is little evidence they converted anyone.

front: What were the effects of the Marian burnings and the exile of Protestants?
p1: c.800 Protestants fled to Germany and Switzerland in early 1554 — including many printers who kept Cranmer's Prayer Book and Foxe's Book of Martyrs in circulation.
p2: The exiles included many who had become more radical in Protestant hotspots — they would return to challenge Elizabeth's via media from a Calvinist perspective.
p3: John Foxe's Book of Martyrs highlighted the burnings and shaped how posterity viewed the Marian regime. Many people viewed the burnings as entertainment or a commercial opportunity — there is little evidence they converted the audience.

front: What specific evidence shows the limits of Mary's Catholic restoration?
p1: Edward's short reign meant much of the country, especially the North, had always remained Catholic. Most church records identify that Catholic worship returned speedily and many welcomed it.
p2: Unlike Henry and Edward, Mary faced no rebellion on the issue of religion — Wyatt's was primarily about the Spanish marriage. Over 800 clergy were deprived for failing to return to Catholic practices — though a small proportion of the total.
p3: Five years was insufficient to enact lasting change. By not producing an heir, Catholicism did not triumph. But the time it took Elizabeth to re-establish Protestantism suggests the Marian restoration had real de facto impact.

front: What were the causes of the Great Price Rise — population and harvest?
p1: From 1525–1551 the population rose from 2.3 to 3 million — agricultural productivity could not keep pace, so food prices rose.
p2: Bad harvests were worsened by the end of the Medieval Warm Period and beginning of the Little Ice Age. Many years failed to provide sufficient food even for subsistence farming.
p3: Surplus population led to rising prices and rents (increased demand for land) and declining wages — creating a Malthusian crisis that led to famine and disease.

front: What were the causes of the Great Price Rise — debasement and enclosure?
p1: Debasement: Henry VIII reduced the precious metal content of coinage to fund wars — this reduced confidence in the currency and prices rose to compensate. Somerset continued debasement to fund the Scottish war.
p2: Enclosure: growing cloth market led gentry to convert arable land to livestock — less food produced, more unemployment. Gentry also practiced rack renting and regrating to exploit the poor.
p3: Spanish Bullion: gold and silver from the New World decreased the value of precious metals across Europe — making coinage less valuable and exacerbating price rises.

front: What was the impact of the Great Price Rise?
p1: High levels of poverty and vagrancy. The Vagrancy Act of 1547 condemned vagrants to two years slavery for the first offence and lifetime slavery for a second.
p2: There was limited support of the poor since Henry's dissolution of the monasteries had removed a key source of poor relief.
p3: Commonwealth men blamed the Great Price Rise on enclosure and greedy gentlemen — adding to complaints about rack renting and regrating. This misdiagnosis meant the government could not tackle the underlying causes.

front: What were Edward's government socioeconomic policies and how effective were they?
p1: Somerset commissioned John Hales to investigate enclosures in 1548 — contributing to his reputation as the 'Good Duke' but raising expectations he could not fulfil.
p2: Somerset's proclamations and commissions raised hopes amongst the people that he was their champion — but he simultaneously continued debasement to fund the Scottish war, making the economic crisis worse.
p3: The lack of a strong royal presence in the minority meant central government appeared weak and susceptible to rebellion. There was limited poor relief since the Dissolution had removed the Church as a source of charity.

front: How widespread was the unrest of 1549 and what caused it?
p1: 1549 was the 'year of the many-headed monster' — unrest in over half the counties of England, the most widespread of the Tudor period.
p2: The evidence suggests long-term economic changes were the primary cause, but also religion — Somerset's proclamations raised hopes, and the minority made central government appear weak.
p3: Most risings were suppressed by local gentry — only Kett's and the Western Rebellion needed royal suppression. Neither attempted to march on London or overthrow the Crown.

front: What were the causes and early events of Kett's Rebellion?
p1: Began when a mob attacked the enclosures of John Flowerdew, who redirected the protest to Robert Kett — another gentleman who had enclosed land. Rebels soon numbered 16,000.
p2: Demands focused on enclosure and high rents — and also absent or uneducated clergy. In Norwich 6% owned 60% of the land.
p3: 16,000 rebels met in July 1549, marched on Norwich, camped at Mousehold Heath and stormed the city. Kett ran a well-ordered camp — justice was administered to show they could maintain order.

front: How was Kett's Rebellion defeated and how serious was it?
p1: Government sent 14,000 troops. Earl Warwick came and massacred the rebels at Dussindale — 3,000 were killed and 49 leaders executed for treason.
p2: Kett made the fatal error of abandoning his well-defended camp at Mousehold Heath to meet Warwick at Dussindale on open ground — Warwick had 12,000 well-trained troops from the Scottish war.
p3: The rebellion was serious — it captured Norwich, the second largest city. But the rebels never attempted to march on London and their demands were written politely to Somerset, suggesting they believed central government would support them.

front: What were the specific triggers and demands of the Western Rebellion?
p1: The murder of William Body in 1548 — tasked with supervising iconoclasm in Cornwall — and opposition to the First Book of Common Prayer triggered the rebellion. Many Cornishmen were more familiar with Latin than English.
p2: The rebels' demands were almost entirely religious — drawn up by literate local clergy. But demands excluded by the clergy included complaints about high taxes and rents.
p3: At Bodmin the rebels chanted 'Kill all the gentlemen!' — showing economic grievances existed beneath the religious demands. The rebellion was different from Kett's: primarily religious not economic.

front: How was the Western Rebellion defeated and how serious was it?
p1: Rebels gathered at Sampford Courtenay, attacked gentry at St Michael's Mount, Bodmin and Trematon Castle, and besieged Exeter for a month.
p2: A government force of 8,000 led by Lord John Russell defeated the rebels at Sampford Courtenay. Over 3,000 were executed.
p3: The rebellion failed due to no clear leadership — different sections attacked different targets. Like Kett's, the rebels never attempted to march on London. Both rebellions together show 1549 was the most serious crisis of the Tudor period — but also the limits of mid-Tudor unrest.

front: What were the causes of Wyatt's Rebellion in January 1554?
p1: The ostensible cause was Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain — concerns over foreign patronage, entanglement in Habsburg wars and xenophobia. Timing immediately after the marriage was proposed in parliament supports this.
p2: However xenophobia may have masked other causes. The rebellion began in Protestant Kent — part of the plot was to replace Mary with Elizabeth. Many leaders had lost court positions due to their faith.
p3: Collapse of the cloth trade created unemployment in Kent. A plot was developed between Wyatt, Sir James Croft and Sir Peter Carew for a four-pronged attack — discovered when Courtenay disclosed it to Gardiner.

front: What were the key events of Wyatt's Rebellion?
p1: Only Wyatt in Kent rose — he raised 3,000 men and marched on London. A government force led by the Duke of Norfolk was sent but the soldiers deserted and joined Wyatt declaring 'We are all Englishmen!'.
p2: Wyatt reached the gates of London. Mary gave an impassioned Guildhall speech which secured the Londoners' support — they refused to open the city gates. The rebellion was defeated.
p3: Wyatt and leaders were executed. Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower — released after Wyatt refused to implicate her under torture. Lady Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were executed as a consequence.

front: What were the key events that caused Wyatt's Rebellion to fail?
p1: Government soldiers deserted Norfolk and joined Wyatt — if the Londoners had opened the city gates the rebellion could have succeeded. Wyatt was potentially very close to victory.
p2: Only one of the planned four forces actually rose — the other leaders got cold feet. The rebellion was poorly coordinated and lacked popular support outside Kent.
p3: Mary's decisive Guildhall speech was crucial — it showed female rule need not be weak. Mary proceeded with the marriage to Philip despite the rebellion, demonstrating her determination.

front: What domestic religious pressures did Elizabeth face in 1558?
p1: Returning Marian exiles had been radicalised by Calvinist and Zwinglian ideas in Zurich, Frankfurt and Geneva — denying any role for the monarch in the Church.
p2: The powerful bishops Elizabeth inherited from Mary were all Catholics. Approximately 1/3 of the powerful English nobility and gentry retained the Catholic faith privately.
p3: Under Mary's reign Catholicism had been restored by law. Elizabeth's personal beliefs: raised Protestant but found radical Protestantism tedious and had a fondness for ceremonial aspects of Catholicism.

front: What international religious pressures did Elizabeth face in 1558?
p1: Spain and France were both strongly Catholic. The Habsburg-Valois rivalry meant they despised each other — Elizabeth's political future depended on this rivalry continuing.
p2: Scotland was a complication — Mary Queen of Scots was married to the French Dauphin Francis. Henry II of France presented Mary as the true Queen of England — a figure unifying Scotland, France and England against Elizabeth.
p3: Many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce. In 1559 Scottish Protestant Lords overthrew Mary of Guise and made Scotland Protestant.

front: What were the key provisions of the Act of Supremacy (1559)?
p1: Removed the Pope's authority over the English Church. Made Elizabeth Supreme Governor of the Church — not 'Supreme Head' as Henry had been, to avoid offending those who believed a woman could not be Head of the Church.
p2: Elizabeth was in charge of a strict episcopal hierarchy of Archbishops and Bishops.
p3: Mary's heresy laws were repealed — no more burnings.

front: What were the key provisions of the Act of Uniformity (1559)?
p1: Cranmer's 1552 Book of Common Prayer used in all churches — but the 'Black Rubric' that explicitly denied Transubstantiation was omitted, leaving the question deliberately ambiguous.
p2: During Holy Communion, wording from both the 1552 and the more conservative 1548 Prayer Books was used — allowing open interpretation of Transubstantiation or Consubstantiation.
p3: Everyone must attend a licensed Church of England church on a Sunday — recusancy fine of 1 shilling (average weekly wage of a labourer).

front: What did the Royal Injunctions of 1559 establish?
p1: Church taxes (First Fruits and Tenths) were to be paid to the Crown. The few small monasteries that Mary had managed to restore were dissolved again.
p2: The clergy were to wear distinctive vestments. Music was encouraged at services and images (statues and stained glass) were accepted.
p3: The clergy could marry. Elizabeth described the settlement as Via Media — 'the middle way' — designed to be an acceptable compromise that would cease religious conflict.

front: What obstacles did Elizabeth face getting the Settlement through Parliament in 1559?
p1: Catholic bishops and Catholic lay nobles in the House of Lords showed they would oppose the settlement — particularly objecting to making Elizabeth 'Head of the Church'.
p2: Elizabeth prorogued parliament over Easter 1559 to delay. She arrested the Bishops of Lincoln and Winchester and compromised by adopting the title 'Supreme Governor'.
p3: The Settlement passed the House of Lords by just three votes. Elizabeth then removed the Marian bishops when they refused to swear the Oath of Loyalty.

front: What were the specific Puritan challenges in Parliament — Strickland and Cope?
p1: John Neale argued that a small organised 'Puritan Choir' attempted to alter the settlement through Parliament — though other historians suggest Puritan influence only increased in the 1600s.
p2: Strickland's Proposals (1571): Walter Strickland attempted to alter the Book of Common Prayer to remove vestments, the ring in marriage and kneeling at communion. Summoned before the Privy Council for infringing the Royal Prerogative and barred from parliament.
p3: Cope's Proposals (1586): Anthony Cope MP proposed the 'bill and book' — replacing the Book of Common Prayer with the Genevan Prayer Book and removing the episcopacy. Cope and four supporters were sent to the Tower. The bill was defeated.

front: What were the Vestiarian Controversy and the challenge from Cartwright?
p1: The Vestiarian Controversy: Puritans despised vestments as signifying clergy to be holy men separate from ordinary worshippers. Matthew Parker's 1566 Advertisements compromised — but 37 clergymen who refused lost their jobs.
p2: The 39 Articles — central ordinances of the Church of England — were agreed at the Convocation of 1563 but resisted by Puritans as not radical enough. In 1571 it was conceded clergy with reservations need not follow ceremonial articles, but all had to follow doctrinal articles.
p3: Thomas Cartwright gave Presbyterian lectures at Cambridge in 1570, strongly denouncing Church hierarchy — he lost his professorship and his freedom of speech.

front: What were the Admonition to Parliament, Marprelate Tracts and Separatist movements?
p1: Admonition to Parliament (1572): Field and Wilcox penned a public criticism of parliament calling for the end of Church episcopacy — imprisoned for a year but the Admonition circulated amongst the literate population.
p2: Marprelate Tracts (1588–89): series of Puritan pamphlets under the pseudonym Martin Marprelate making vicious attacks on bishops — alienated many moderates and allowed the Privy Council to suppress the printing presses.
p3: 1581 Brownist Church led by Robert Browne in Norwich — suppressed. 1590s: Henry Barrow and John Greenwood led a new Separatist movement in London — leaders arrested and executed in 1593. Puritanism survived through prophesyings, the classis movement and the protection of councillors like Leicester.

front: What were Matthew Parker's key actions as Archbishop (1559–75)?
p1: Parker had previously been Anne Boleyn's chaplain — a Protestant who had not gone into exile during Mary's reign and was not radicalised by Calvinism or Zwinglism.
p2: Parker defended the Religious Settlement by overseeing the passage of the 39 Articles at the Convocation of 1563 — resisting Puritan attempts to introduce more radical changes. These changes were defeated by a single vote.
p3: Parker reached a compromise with Puritans during the Vestiarian Controversy in his 1566 Advertisements — conceding that clergy could wear simply a 'comely surplice with long sleeves' at Communion.

front: What were Grindal's and Whitgift's key actions as Archbishop?
p1: Edmund Grindal (1575–83): a former Marian exile sympathetic to Puritan concerns. Came into conflict with Elizabeth over prophesyings — ordered to suppress them in 1576, he refused. Suspended in 1577 and confined to house arrest until his death in 1583.
p2: John Whitgift (1583–1604): used the Court of High Commission to root out non-conformists. Used the Three Articles as a test — clergy had to swear Elizabeth had sovereignty over Church matters, the Book of Common Prayer was the only one to be used, and the 39 Articles were agreeable to God.
p3: Around 300 Puritan clergy were removed by Whitgift's methods. Whitgift showed determined repression could contain but not eliminate the Puritan challenge — Elizabeth supported Whitgift and died holding his hand.

front: Why was the Catholic threat limited before 1568?
p1: Elizabeth's relative tolerance: the heresy laws were repealed — the sole recusancy punishment was a 1 shilling fine. Many Church Papists attended Church of England services before attending secret Catholic services. Elizabeth 'would not open windows unto men's souls'.
p2: Philip of Spain persuaded Pope Pius IV not to excommunicate Elizabeth in 1563 — Philip feared France gaining control of England if Catholic Mary Queen of Scots came to the throne.
p3: The Habsburg-Valois rivalry prevented coordinated Catholic action — 1562–98 the French Wars of Religion raged and 1566–1648 Spain was attempting to suppress the Protestant Dutch Revolt.

front: What were the events of the Rising of the North (1569–70)?
p1: A plot to marry Mary to the Duke of Norfolk to strengthen her claim to the English throne was uncovered. The Catholic northern earls of Northumberland and Westmoreland launched an uprising.
p2: The rebels captured Durham and held Catholic Latin mass in the Cathedral. A summons was issued to other Catholic nobility and gentry — none answered the call.
p3: A royal army led by the Earl of Sussex marched north and the rebels fled without fighting a battle. Mary was moved to Coventry. Elizabeth executed 450 rebels.

front: What was the significance of Mary Queen of Scots' arrival in England and the Papal Bull of 1570?
p1: When Mary returned to Scotland in 1561 she found it ruled by Protestant Lords. She was forced to abdicate in 1567 following suspected involvement in the assassination of Lord Darnley. In 1568 Mary fled to northern England seeking Elizabeth's support — placed under house arrest.
p2: Mary was a real danger — Elizabeth's cousin, next in line, and if she succeeded she would likely restore Catholicism. Her arrival in the highly Catholic North provided a figurehead around which Catholic plots would ferment.
p3: In 1570, Pope Pius V issued his Papal bull Regnans in Excelsis excommunicating Elizabeth — Catholics were now absolved of any loyalty to her. This transformed the Catholic threat from passive non-conformity to active potential treachery.

front: What were the three main Catholic plots against Elizabeth?
p1: 1571 — Ridolfi Plot: Catholic banker Ridolfi plotted with the Pope, Philip II and the Duke of Norfolk to marry Mary to Norfolk and provoke a Catholic uprising. Discovered by Cecil. Norfolk executed 1572 but Elizabeth resisted calls to execute Mary.
p2: 1583 — Throckmorton Plot: plot to liberate Mary and overthrow Elizabeth, involving the Duke of Guise, Philip II, the Pope and William Allen's seminary priests. Uncovered by Walsingham's spies.
p3: 1586 — Babington Plot: plot involving Elizabeth's assassination and Spanish-French invasion. Walsingham discovered evidence directly implicating Mary herself. Parliament petitioned for Mary's execution — she was executed in February 1587.

front: What was the Bond of Association (1584) and the Treaty of Joinville?
p1: 1584 — Bond of Association agreed by the Privy Council: anyone linked to future plots against Elizabeth would be executed. This was a proactive measure rather than simply reacting to plots.
p2: 1584 — Treaty of Joinville: Spanish and French Catholics joined together against Protestantism — showing the potential for coordinated Catholic action if the Habsburg-Valois rivalry were resolved.
p3: Parliament repeatedly pushed for Mary's execution in 1572, 1585 and 1586. The combined pressure of the Lords, Commons and Privy Council following the Babington Plot finally forced Elizabeth's hand in 1587.

front: What were the seminary priests and Jesuits and how did they operate?
p1: William Allen's 'English College' at Douai in France produced the first seminary priests — they arrived in England from 1574. By 1585, 279 had travelled to England.
p2: The Jesuits were another order who arrived in the 1580s to restore Catholicism. In total, around 650 Jesuits or seminary priests were active in England — many sheltered by Catholic nobility and gentry in priest holes.
